--- title: "Simulation as a method" subtitle: "Synthetic data with a known recipe" bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib] --- This is the simulation module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd), and it is optional. Most quantitative pages on this site analyse data that came from the world; this module analyses data that came from a recipe written in advance, so that the answer is known before any model runs. That inversion, known as fake-data simulation, is a standard habit in applied statistics. *Regression and Other Stories* uses it constantly, on the argument that fitting models to data whose coefficients you planted yourself is how you learn what your models can and cannot recover [@GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories]. The same habit underpins classroom practice [@GelmanVehtari2024ActiveStatisticsStories] and the workflow literature, where experimentation on simulated data is one of the named components of model-building [@GelmanEtAl2026BayesianWorkflow]. The module simulates the field experiment of the housing-audit case, whose design is simple enough to write down in a few lines: an audit whose true gap you set, then recover, then break by letting the name change who replies, and then use to count how often a study of its size finds the gap. Participants meet the questions behind it in Part 4 of the [one-day course with a methods focus](../tracks/housing-one-day-methods/part-4.qmd), where the power of the original study and of the replication is compared, and in [stage 4](../tracks/self-study/stage-4.qmd) of the self-study route. The simulations are declared and diagnosed with DeclareDesign [@BlairEtAl2023DeclareDesignDeclareDiagnose], an R package that describes a research design in four parts, which its authors call the model, the inquiry, the data strategy and the answer strategy. The **model** is the recipe, the description of the units and of how each would respond to each condition. The **inquiry** is the quantity that the study is meant to learn, its estimand. The **data strategy** says how the units are sampled and assigned, and the **answer strategy** is the estimator. Declared that way, a design can be run as often as one likes, and the package summarises the runs: how far the estimates fall from the estimand on average, how widely they scatter, how often the interval covers the truth, and how often the test rejects. The simulations with many draws ran once, in scripts in `companion/_model-outputs/` of the source repository, and the page reads their results; every declaration on the page runs when it is built. ## 1. A recipe for an audit {#sec-recipe} The original authors (OAs) of the housing-audit case emailed public housing authorities from names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant and coded whether each reply opened with the name of the sender [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. The claim compares the Hispanic and the white names, and the recipe below takes its numbers from the 665 delivered emails to those names in `housing_audit.csv`. In the data, 54.9% of the authorities replied, and among the coded replies 61.1% of those to white names and 41.2% of those to Hispanic names opened with the name, a gap of −20.0 points. The first recipe plants that gap and nothing else. Each authority would reply or not whatever the name, so that the chance of a reply is the same 54.9% for both. Among the authorities that reply, a white name is greeted by name with the probability observed for white names and a Hispanic name with the probability observed for Hispanic names, and an official who would greet the Hispanic name by name would also greet the white one. Each authority therefore carries two potential outcomes, the greeting that it would give each name, and the experiment reveals one of them. The names are assigned by complete random assignment to as many emails as in the experiment, and the answer strategy is the estimator of the case: the difference in the proportions of named greetings among the replies, with HC2 errors. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_delivered <- nrow(audit) n_hispanic <- sum(audit$group == "hispanic") reply_all <- mean(audit$reply) greet_white <- mean(coded$named[coded$group == "white"]) greet_hisp <- mean(coded$named[coded$group == "hispanic"]) # Z = 1 is a Hispanic name; G_Z_0 and G_Z_1 are the greetings that an authority # would give a white and a Hispanic name if it replied recovery <- DeclareDesign::declare_model( N = n_delivered, v = runif(N), u = runif(N), R = as.integer(v < reply_all), G_Z_0 = as.integer(u < greet_white), G_Z_1 = as.integer(u < greet_hisp) ) + DeclareDesign::declare_inquiry(gap = mean(G_Z_1[R == 1] - G_Z_0[R == 1])) + DeclareDesign::declare_assignment(Z = randomizr::complete_ra(N, m = n_hispanic)) + DeclareDesign::declare_measurement(G = fabricatr::reveal_outcomes(G ~ Z)) + DeclareDesign::declare_estimator(G ~ Z, .method = estimatr::lm_robust, se_type = "HC2", subset = R == 1, inquiry = "gap", term = "Z", label = "among replies") DeclareDesign::draw_data(recovery) |> head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 8 ID v u R G_Z_0 G_Z_1 Z G 1 001 0.0981 0.415 1 1 0 1 0 2 002 0.429 0.423 1 1 0 0 1 3 003 0.242 0.668 1 0 0 0 0 4 004 0.683 0.168 0 1 1 1 1 5 005 0.358 0.446 1 1 0 1 0 6 006 0.0102 0.0629 1 1 1 0 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} DeclareDesign::run_design(recovery) |> datawizard::data_select(select = c("inquiry", "estimand", "estimate", "std.error", "p.value")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 inquiry estimand estimate std.error p.value 1 gap -0.205 -0.131 0.0520 0.0121 ``` ::: ::: The first table shows six simulated authorities with both of their potential greetings, the name that the draw assigned them and the greeting that the experiment would record. The second is one run of the whole design: the planted gap among the authorities that replied in this draw (the estimand), the estimate from the replies, its standard error and its p-value. One run is one experiment, and it says nothing yet about the estimator. The planted value is known, but a single estimate that lands near it, or far from it, could be luck. ## 2. Recovery across draws {#sec-recover} The estimator is judged by what it does over many runs of the same design. The script `simulate_audit.R` runs this one 2,000 times: ```r DeclareDesign::diagnose_design(recovery, sims = 2000) ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The estimates of the gap in named greetings in 2,000 simulated audits whose recipe plants the gap of the original study and lets the name change nothing else. The burgundy line marks the planted gap, and the dashed line the gap that the original study found. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/sim_audit_draws.csv`.](simulation_files/figure-html/fig-recovery-1.png){#fig-recovery fig-alt='A bell-shaped histogram of simulated gaps centred on about −20 points and spreading from about −37 to −3 points; the planted gap and the observed gap of the study lie together near its centre.' width=672} ::: ::: Over the 2,000 draws the estimates average −19.97 points against a planted gap of −19.98, so that the estimator is unbiased for this recipe to within the noise of the simulation. Their standard deviation, 5.19 points, is the sampling error of a study of this size, which no single study can observe, and the standard error that the case reports for its one real estimate, 5.16 points, is an estimate of it. The 95% interval covered the planted gap in 96.7% of the draws, close to the 95% that it promises, and the test rejected a gap of zero in 96.9% of them. A real study is one draw from a distribution like this one, and the dashed line shows where the original study fell in it. Recovery is the first check of any estimator, and it is the one that the course runs implicitly whenever it calls an estimator unbiased. It holds only for the recipe that was written. The next section changes the recipe in the one respect that the data of the case cannot check. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Try it Copy the declaration of `recovery` into your workspace and change one ingredient at a time: halve `n_delivered`, set `greet_hisp` equal to `greet_white`, or lower `reply_all` to a quarter. Diagnose each version with `DeclareDesign::diagnose_design(recovery, sims = 500)` and compare the standard deviation of the estimates, the coverage and the power. Which ingredient changes the bias, and which change only the precision? ::: ## 3. Conditioning on a reply {#sec-reply} The comparison among replies is a pure effect of the name only if the name did not change who replied, an assumption that the [experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) and the [causal-graphs module](dags.qmd#sec-collider) both examine. In the data the Hispanic names drew replies slightly less often, 52.7% against 57.5%. The second recipe builds that difference in. Authorities with a low value of `v` reply to either name, and a band of authorities, 4.8% of them, replies only to a white name. How those marginal repliers greet a white name is not in the data, because their replies to white names cannot be told apart from the others, so the recipe sets it three ways: never by name, as often as the other officials, or always by name. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} reply_white <- mean(audit$reply[audit$group == "white"]) reply_hisp <- mean(audit$reply[audit$group == "hispanic"]) greet_marginal <- greet_white reply_design <- DeclareDesign::declare_model( N = n_delivered, v = runif(N), u = runif(N), always = v < reply_hisp, R_Z_0 = as.integer(v < reply_white), R_Z_1 = as.integer(v < reply_hisp), G_Z_0 = dplyr::if_else(always, as.integer(u < greet_white), as.integer(u < greet_marginal)), G_Z_1 = as.integer(u < greet_hisp), A_Z_0 = R_Z_0 * G_Z_0, A_Z_1 = R_Z_1 * G_Z_1 ) + DeclareDesign::declare_inquiry(gap_always = mean(G_Z_1[always] - G_Z_0[always]), gap_all = mean(A_Z_1 - A_Z_0)) + DeclareDesign::declare_assignment(Z = randomizr::complete_ra(N, m = n_hispanic)) + DeclareDesign::declare_measurement(R = fabricatr::reveal_outcomes(R ~ Z), G = fabricatr::reveal_outcomes(G ~ Z), A = fabricatr::reveal_outcomes(A ~ Z)) + DeclareDesign::declare_estimator(G ~ Z, .method = estimatr::lm_robust, se_type = "HC2", subset = R == 1, inquiry = "gap_always", term = "Z", label = "among replies") + DeclareDesign::declare_estimator(A ~ Z, .method = estimatr::lm_robust, se_type = "HC2", inquiry = "gap_all", term = "Z", label = "all delivered") ``` ::: ```r DeclareDesign::redesign(reply_design, greet_marginal = c(0, greet_white, 1)) |> DeclareDesign::diagnose_design(sims = 2000) ``` The design asks two questions. The first is the effect of the name on the greeting among the authorities that would reply to either name. The second is the effect of the name on whether an email receives a named greeting at all, counted over every delivered email, with an email that drew no reply counting as one without a named greeting. The first is answered by the comparison among replies, the second by the comparison among all delivered emails, the two estimands between which the curve of the case chooses (the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd#sec-forks) sets out how much of the curve that choice carries). ::: {#tbl-reply .cell tbl-cap='The two comparisons over 2,000 simulated audits under each assumption about the authorities that reply only to white names. Estimands and estimates in percentage points; the bias is the mean estimate minus the estimand, and the coverage the share of 95% intervals that contain the estimand. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/sim_audit_diagnosis.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Marginal repliers greet a white name by name Comparison Estimand Mean estimate Bias Coverage
never all delivered −10.6 −10.6 0.0 96.9%
never among replies −20.0 −14.9 5.2 86.8%
as the others, 61% all delivered −13.5 −13.5 0.0 97.7%
as the others, 61% among replies −19.9 −20.0 −0.1 96.8%
always all delivered −15.3 −15.3 −0.0 96.4%
always among replies −19.9 −23.3 −3.4 91.3%
``` ::: ::: The comparison among replies recovers the effect on the authorities that reply to either name in one of the three recipes only, the one in which the marginal repliers greet a white name as the other officials do. If they never greet by name, the replies to white names hold more unnamed greetings than the authorities that reply to either name would give, and the estimate falls short of the planted gap by 5.2 points on average, with an interval that covers the truth in 86.8% of the draws. If they always greet by name, the estimate overshoots by 3.4 points. No amount of data from the experiment distinguishes the three recipes, because each produces data of the same kind. The trimming bounds of the [experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) work from the same premise: they compute, from the observed replies, the range within which the effect on the authorities that reply to either name must lie whatever the marginal repliers do. The comparison among all delivered emails is unbiased in every recipe, because nothing is conditioned on after the names were assigned. Its estimand, however, moves with the recipe, from −15.3 to −10.6 points, because it adds the effect of the name on replying to its effect on the greeting. The two comparisons therefore answer different questions, and the simulation shows the price of each. One answers its own question exactly, and that question mixes two effects of the name. The other answers the narrower question about greetings only under an assumption that the data cannot test. ## 4. Power by simulation {#sec-power} The power of a study is the probability that it rejects a null hypothesis of no effect when an effect of a given size is real. For a difference between two proportions, a formula gives it, and the [experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-power) draws the analytic curves for the comparison among replies of the original study, about 181 replies a group, and of the replication, 369 a group. Simulation gives the same quantity by counting: declare the design with a planted gap, run it many times, and count the share of runs in which the test rejects. The script `simulate_audit.R` does that for gaps of 0 to 25 points below a white rate of 61%, with 1,000 runs for each gap and size. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The power of the comparison among replies at the size of the original study (181 replies a group) and of the replication (369 a group): the share of 1,000 simulated audits in which the HC2 test rejected a gap of zero at the 5% level (points), and the analytic power of a two-sided test of two proportions (lines). Sources: `companion/_model-outputs/sim_audit_diagnosis.csv` and `cases/housing/data/display_power.csv`.](simulation_files/figure-html/fig-power-1.png){#fig-power fig-alt='Two rising curves of power against the planted gap, the replication above the original; the simulated points lie on or very near the analytic lines, and both start near 5% at a gap of zero.' width=672} ::: ::: The simulated points lie on the analytic curves to within the noise of 1,000 runs, which is what a check by simulation should find when the formula fits the design. At a planted gap of zero the share of rejections is the rate of false positives, 3.6% at the original size and 5.2% at the size of the replication. With 1,000 runs a share of about 5% is uncertain by about 0.7 points either way, so the test at the size of the replication holds its 5%, and the test at the original size, with few replies in each group, may reject slightly less often than it promises. The same runs show what no power formula reports directly. At a true gap of 10 points the original design rejects in 52.4% of the runs, and the estimates of the runs that reach significance average −14.5 points, 45% larger than the truth. A study of modest power that reports only its significant results overstates the effect, which is the exaggeration that the experiments module computes from a formula and which the replication, at a larger size, would expose. Randomisation inference, which the experiments module runs with ri2, builds a distribution of the same kind from the observed data without any recipe: it keeps the outcomes and reshuffles the names, so that every reshuffle is a draw from a world in which the names changed nothing. The simulation at a gap of zero writes that world as a recipe instead, and the two agree because both describe what a design of this size produces when there is nothing to find. ## Further reading {#sec-further} For the habit itself, *Regression and Other Stories* is the core text, with short fake-data simulations that recur throughout and build on one another [@GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories], and *Active Statistics* packages the same moves as classroom activities [@GelmanVehtari2024ActiveStatisticsStories]. For declaring a design before the data exist and diagnosing it by simulation, the documentation of DeclareDesign works through experiments, surveys and observational designs in the four parts used in sections 1 to 4 [@BlairEtAl2023DeclareDesignDeclareDiagnose]. For multilevel structures, DeBruine and Barr build a mixed-effects simulation from nothing and recover its parameters, on the argument that constructing the data is how you come to understand the model [@DeBruineBarr2021UnderstandingMixedeffectsModels]. For simulation inside a modelling workflow – prior and posterior predictive checking, calibration, experimentation on synthetic data before touching the real thing – the Bayesian workflow book is the current statement [@GelmanEtAl2026BayesianWorkflow], and its habits transfer well beyond Bayesian settings. And for simulation as a research method in its own right, the design framework of @MorrisEtAl2019UsingSimulationStudies supplies the vocabulary (aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures, stated before the study is run), and the book-length treatment written for social scientists is @CarseyHarden2014MonteCarloSimulation. Simulation studies are analyses too, and they have researcher degrees of freedom of their own – conditions, performance measures, which results get reported – so a comparative study can be tuned until any method looks superior [@PawelEtAl2024PitfallsPotentialsSimulation]. The disciplines that this course keeps returning to, preregistered designs and justified choices, apply to simulated data as much as to real data. The declarations of sections 1 and 3 and the script behind every diagnosis are committed, so the quickest place to begin is the first Try it: change what the recipe plants, run it again, and check what the estimator does when you already know the answer. ## References {.unnumbered} ::: {#refs} :::
